title: 29 FDI Investments Worth ₹4,895.65 Crore Reported Under Revised Framework
subtitle: Revised FDI Framework Facilitates Investment with Non-Controlling Beneficial Ownership from Land Bordering Countries
body_text:
A total of 29 FDI investments have been reported under the revised framework up to 20 August 2026, involving proposed FDI of ₹4,895.65 crore. These investments span a range of sectors, including Information Technology, Artificial Intelligence, Information & Communication, Manufacturing, Pharmaceuticals, Data Centres and Transport Services, among others.
The 29 investments have been reported by investors/entities based in jurisdictions including Mauritius, the United States, the Republic of Korea, Japan, Singapore, Luxembourg and the Cayman Islands.
The revised framework facilitates and expedites the flow of foreign investment into India by removing the requirement of prior Government approval in cases involving non-controlling Land Bordering Countries (LBC) ownership of up to 10%. The reform provides greater certainty to investors, reduces transaction time and further strengthens the ease of doing business in India.
With Press Note 2 of 2026 and the consequent amendment to the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019, notified on 1 May 2026, the beneficial ownership test is now applied at the level of the investor entity. Investors with non-controlling LBC ownership of up to 10% can invest through the automatic route, subject to applicable sectoral caps, entry routes and other conditions. The investor entity can proceed with the investment without obtaining any other approval, after reporting the relevant information to the Government.
Earlier, foreign investors with beneficial ownership from LBCs of India were required to obtain prior Government approval under Press Note 3 of 2020, even where such LBC ownership was very small. This had been a long-standing concern among investors seeking greater clarity and ease of investment.
***
Abhishek Dayal/ Garima Singh/ Ishita Biswas

enrichment.summary: India's revised FDI framework, notified via Press Note 2 of 2026, has facilitated 29 foreign investments worth ₹4,895.65 crore up to 20 August 2026, spanning sectors like IT, AI, manufacturing, pharmaceuticals and data centres. The investments originated from jurisdictions including Mauritius, the US, South Korea, Japan, Singapore, Luxembourg and the Cayman Islands. The reform allows non-controlling beneficial ownership of up to 10% from Land Bordering Countries (LBCs) to enter via the automatic route without prior government approval, subject to sectoral caps and conditions.
enrichment.context:
Press Note 3 of 2020 was introduced by India in April 2020, in the backdrop of the COVID-19 pandemic and heightened border tensions with China, to curb opportunistic takeovers of Indian firms by entities from countries sharing a land border with India (China, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Myanmar, Bhutan, Afghanistan). It mandated prior government approval for any FDI involving beneficial ownership from these countries, regardless of how small the stake was, which investors criticised as overly restrictive since it also affected legitimate, non-controlling minority investments routed through global funds with even minimal LBC-linked ownership (e.g., via Mauritius or Singapore-based funds with some Chinese LPs).

Press Note 2 of 2026 and the corresponding amendment to the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 (notified 1 May 2026) recalibrate this by applying the beneficial ownership test at the investor-entity level rather than tracing every layer of ownership, and by carving out an automatic-route exemption for non-controlling LBC ownership up to 10%. This is part of a broader ease-of-doing-business push and reflects an attempt to balance national security concerns with the need to attract foreign capital, especially as India seeks to position itself as an alternative manufacturing and tech investment destination amid global supply chain diversification.

prelims_questions.question: Press Note 3 of 2020, which mandated prior government approval for FDI from land bordering countries, was primarily introduced in response to concerns regarding:
options: Opportunistic takeovers of Indian companies during the COVID-19 pandemic
prelims_questions.explanation: Press Note 3 of 2020 was introduced amid the COVID-19 pandemic to prevent opportunistic acquisitions of financially stressed Indian companies by entities from countries sharing a land border with India, particularly China.

prelims_questions.question: As per the revised FDI framework under Press Note 2 of 2026, non-controlling beneficial ownership from Land Bordering Countries up to what percentage can invest via the automatic route without prior government approval?
prelims_questions.explanation: The revised framework allows non-controlling LBC ownership of up to 10% to invest through the automatic route, subject to sectoral caps and conditions, without requiring prior government approval.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the rationale behind Press Note 3 of 2020 and critically examine the implications of its recent relaxation through Press Note 2 of 2026 for India's foreign investment climate and national security considerations.

Balancing national security concerns with the imperative of attracting foreign direct investment is a persistent policy challenge for India. Discuss with reference to India's FDI policy vis-à-vis countries sharing a land border with it.

study_notes.reason: The release carries a testable factual core (Press Note 3 of 2020, Press Note 2 of 2026, the 10% non-controlling LBC threshold, investor-entity level test) and genuine analytical depth on balancing national security with ease-of-doing-business and FDI attractiveness amid supply chain diversification.

prelims.point: Press Note 3 of 2020 mandated prior government approval for any FDI involving beneficial ownership from Land Bordering Countries (LBCs), regardless of stake size.
prelims.why_important: A frequently cited FDI policy landmark; aspirants must know its origin (2020, China border tensions/COVID) and its blanket approval requirement.

prelims.point: Press Note 2 of 2026 permits non-controlling LBC ownership up to 10% to enter via the automatic route without prior government approval, subject to sectoral caps.
prelims.why_important: This is the specific numerical threshold and route change UPSC could test as the defining feature of the 2026 reform.

prelims.point: The beneficial ownership test under the revised framework is applied at the level of the investor entity, not by tracing every layer of ownership.
prelims.why_important: This is the key conceptual shift distinguishing Press Note 2 of 2026 from Press Note 3 of 2020, likely to feature in a comparison-based question.

prelims.point: LBCs as defined under India's FDI policy include China, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Myanmar, Bhutan and Afghanistan.
prelims.why_important: Aspirants should know which countries fall under the LBC classification since it determines the approval route applicability.

prelims.point: The framework operates under the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019, amended on 1 May 2026.
prelims.why_important: Identifies the legal instrument through which FDI policy changes are operationalised, distinct from Press Notes which are policy statements under FEMA.

mains.point: Press Note 3 of 2020 was criticised as overly restrictive because it also captured legitimate minority investments routed through global funds with minimal LBC-linked ownership.
mains.theme: Balancing national security with investment ease
mains.analytical_use: Useful for a question on evaluating unintended consequences of security-driven FDI restrictions on legitimate capital flows.

mains.point: The 2026 recalibration reflects an attempt to balance national security concerns with the need to attract foreign capital amid global supply chain diversification.
mains.analytical_use: Core argument for a 'Discuss/Examine' question on how India recalibrates security-driven trade/investment restrictions without compromising economic openness.

mains.point: The reform is positioned as part of a broader ease-of-doing-business push, reducing transaction time and providing greater investor certainty.
mains.analytical_use: Supports answers on governance reforms aimed at improving India's investment climate and reducing regulatory friction.

mains.point: The reform can be read as India positioning itself as an alternative manufacturing and tech investment destination amid global supply chain diversification away from China.
mains.analytical_use: Relevant for international relations/economy questions on India's strategy to benefit from China+1 and supply chain realignment.

low_priority.reason: Illustrative data without standalone significance; unlikely to be tested as these are generic FDI source countries.

low_priority.point: The exact figures of 29 investments and ₹4,895.65 crore.
low_priority.reason: Time-bound statistical detail with no lasting examinable value beyond the date given.

low_priority.point: Sectoral spread (IT, AI, manufacturing, pharma, data centres, transport) of the reported investments.
low_priority.reason: Descriptive listing without deeper analytical or factual testability.
